major periods of upheaval coupled with the creation of hybrid cultures under Greek and Roman conquests. These new groups had very different views about the enculturated body and the body in death. Patterns may be discerned in terms of temporal change and on the basis of sex, age, and class. The general pattern of elaboration outlined above can now be tested against the specific cemeteries and individual tombs of Deir el Medina-throughout the New Kingdom and beyond. Many Egyptologists would claim that the site is unrepresentative and its data unusable, yet it is one of the few coherent data sets we possess for the pharaonic period. Moreover, the entire issue of what constitutes a representative sample is open to question. A study of 25 well documented tombs from various sectors of the Deir el Medina cemeteries allows certain propositions to be made about the treatment and elaboration of mummified bodies throughout the New Kingdom. Overall, the preparation of bodies was less elaborate than one would expect, varying widely according to factors such as age, sex, and socioeconomic group. In the Eastern Necropolis children were often buried in rags or a single cloth, without embalming, and were subsequently reduced to a skeletal state (e.g., tombs 1372, 1374, and 1375).47 In 1372, however, one girl had three layers of wrappings and in 1382 another girl had five layers, so that treatment was individual and variable rather than standardized. Older individuals of both sexes rarely display any organ removal, but many bodies were shaven and hairless, as in the 18th Dynasty tombs 1370, 1379, and 1388.48 As for wrappings and shrouds, individuals often had eight or nine layers, or as many as 15; the number varied significantly between occupants of a single tomb. Bruyere commented that these poorer individuals were also buried without natron or resinous treatments. As a generalizing trend, the treatment of male and female adult bodies at this lower social stratum is egalitarian, which parallels their tomb goods and other provisions for the afterlife. The situation was markedly different for individuals from the wealthier, higher-status tombs in the Western Necropolis. Among the 18th-20th Dynasty individuals there, significant differences were based on age and sex (tombs with mixed contents from later periods are considered below). In the 18th Dynasty tomb 1159A, Sennefer has 14 layers of wrappings with a mask, while the accompanying female is poorly wrapped and consequently reduced to a skeleton. From the same period in the tomb of Kha (tomb 8), the male owner is well wrapped and in much better condition than his wife Merit. According to Bruyere, none of these bodies shows the removal of the brain or organs, nor treatment with natron. In the Ramesside tomb 336 of Neferrenpet there were some 74 bodies, the majority of which show an incision in the stomach. Some bodies were embalmed only with natron, others with resin. Sometimes the viscera were in natron and placed between the thighs. Bruyere recorded individuals with six to ten layers of wrappings for the most part. In the tomb of Sennedjem (tomb 1), he recorded that the bodies were also poorly embalmed, suggesting that this was a widespread phenomenon even among the elite of the community. Although Egyptian bodily practices were an integral part of the burial process, other factors such as the tomb complex, its decoration, provision of tomb goods, and magico-ritual elements absorbed more time and expense in total. In the Graeco-Roman period we generally witness a complete inversion of burial practices at Deir el Medina. The external focus on display collapses into an exclusive focus on the presentation of the mummified body itself, particularly the elaboration of the linen wrappings and decoration. For example, linen wrappings in the New Kingdom are largely undecorated, whereas they become elaborately colored and decorated in later times. The painted shroud from tomb 1447, now in Leiden, is a pertinent example. These linens were very costly and, in Roman times, such burials should be regarded as expensive both in terms of materials and actual preparation. In sum, we see a difference in bodily praxis in the 18th Dynasty on the basis of cemetery location and social level. Then we have marked diachronic change in bodily treatments from the 18th Dynasty to the Ramesside period, extending on to Greek and Roman times. To quote in extenso from Quirke: Mummification combines a physical preservation of the body, to keep it the same, with the anticipation of a spiritual afterlife, to transfigure the person and make him or her new and different, 'radiant'. Since the efforts to preserve a lifelike outer appearance can only be said to be partially successful, they were supplemented by plaster modelling of facial features and limbs in the third millennium and by packing the skin with stuffing in the early first millennium BC. The art of embalming reached its creative peak in Thebes in the eleventh and tenth centuries BC; in the Ptolemaic and Roman Periods stress was lain instead on the neat outer wrapping of the bandages, often concealing an alarming assortment of limbs within.... From c. 2000 BC the head might be covered with a mask made of linen layers stiffened with plaster, a papier miche effect called cartonnage ... and in the ninth to eighth centuries BC and again in the Ptolemaic Period the wooden coffin was replaced by a cartonnage case that entirely enclosed the mummy.
Treatments of the body such as mummification were not simply measures of preservation; rather, they transfigured the body and imbued it with magical qualities. Perishable bodily substances were replaced by eternal ones held within the mummy cover, which acted as a kind of magic garment. The Egyptian term for mummy, s'h, also means noble or dignitary and signifies the elevation of the deceased's status through the process of transfiguration. Evidence from the long time span of Deir el Medina, from the New Kingdom to the Graeco-Roman period, confirms Assmann's statement that the "mummycase itself gradually evolved into increasingly lavishly decorated stucco-cartonnage and wooden anthropoid coffins, whereby pictorial motifs and decoration patterns merely represent an iconographic formulation of the exact same akh-sphere which is expressed in funerary literature by means of the spoken and written word." From Ramesside times onward, the coffin itself was covered in texts such as excerpts from the underworld descriptions, and two important formulas from the Book of the Dead (Going out by Day and Opening the Tomb, and the formula for causing the ba to unite with the corpse in the underworld). In the 21st Dynasty the decoration on wooden coffins reached its peak. It was also a period of experimentation, where the visual triumphs over the written word. The increasing focus on the body, its preparation and transcendence, and its immediate covering (wrappings and coffin) reached its pinnacle in the Roman period, as evidenced by various burials at Deir el Medina such as the Roman family burial in house C (tomb 1407). This is a particularly rich burial of nine individuals: some of the bodies revealed gilding and even the child Sarapias had some 42 layers of linen wrapping and shrouds. With Roman Egypt we witness the last major revision of the funerary tradition, characterized by an increased focus on the representation of the individual and the individual body through portraiture and painted shrouds.
For Deir el Medina it is possible to study how practices that developed in the Ramesside period were perpetuated and consolidated in later periods. The public and rich character of such mausoleums makes them a natural target for attack by those who do not share, or are indifferent to, the status and values of their builders."'59 It is axiomatic that tombs and monuments were regularly pillaged, remodeled, and usurped throughout pharaonic history. Oddly, this widespread practice existed in a culture that supposedly revered, and feared, their dead. While plundering may have been infrequent within a single period (e.g., the 18th Dynasty) because descendants of the deceased were close at hand, it was more common between periods (e.g., Ptolemaic opening of New Kingdom tombs). At Deir el Medina, tomb reuse was generally confined to the Western Necropolis tombs and those to the north of the site, which represent the larger, more complex tombs from the site. The smaller, less prestigious tombs of the Eastern Necropolis were disregarded. They were inferior in terms of location, construction, size, and orientation. Given the substantial and complex nature of the reused tombs and later finds, it is worth briefly charting the archaeology of post-New Kingdom Deir el Medina. Bruyere's focus during excavation was upon the site in the New Kingdom, yet he still recorded a significant amount of later material deposited in reused tombs in the Western Necropolis. The sphere of death is paramount and this is reflected in the elaborate treatment of the body and coffin at the expense of the traditional concept of a burial assemblage. Even shabtis, typically common for the Third Intermediate period and Late period as the tomb artifact par excellence, diminished and eventually disappeared by Graeco-Roman times.
Later groups evidently felt the landscape of Deir el Medina to be sacred or potent, especially since the Western Necropolis was carpeted with small pyramids and other funerary superstructures. Such a mortuary vision must have been layered with meanings, though not necessarily coherent ones for the original New Kingdom occupants or their successors. It would be wrong to conflate these patterns of reuse as a practice related to the specificities of social memory. These practices were not exclusive to Deir el Medina: evidence from the Valley of the Nobles demonstrates extensive post-New Kingdom reuse of tombs. Much of this activity might have been generated by the choachytes, the libation pourers of nearby Djeme, who were most active in the Ptolemaic period. They maintained the mortuary cult of the local people of Djeme, burying them in local tombs and providing regular cultic offerings. Such activities brought them to Deir el Medina to reuse the numerous tombs at the deserted site. This explains the depositions of scores of anonymous bodies of this period. The nature and density of material supports the notion of significant patterns of later usage, which can be grouped into three types: scattered intrusive finds; domestic reuse of tombs (primarily in Late Antique times); and significant occupation and tomb remodeling.
The first category, scattered intrusive finds, generally consists of Graeco-Roman and Late Antique ceramics (tombs 1150, 1346, 1440, 1450, and 1451),64 papyri (tomb 1446), shabtis (tombs 336 and 1006), decorated linen (tombs 330, 1060, 1447, and 1450), and isolated coffins (tombs 1022 and 1006). These individual finds are testimony to the type of individuals and practices present at Deir el Medina. For example, there is an unusual Roman coffin in 1022 illustrated by Bruyere, described as having leaf motifs and a bird-headed human figure in brown paint on a lime-washed base. Several pieces of Late Antique cloth in tomb 1450 are also quite distinctive: one cloth with an indigo design dates to the third century A.D. and another with floral motifs from the fifth century A.D.
The second category, domestic reuse of extant tombs, is especially noticeable in the Western Necropolis and around the temple of Hathor to the north of the site. This may relate to the proximity of the temple of Hathor as a potent ritual locale with funerary associations. In the Western Necropolis tombs such as 1138 and 1233 were remodeled into structures resembling catacombs in the Late period and Ptolemaic period, respectively. In the region of the temple, tomb 1438 demonstrates both Late Antique and Muslim-period alterations, while tomb 1437 was also reused by Christians, who replastered the walls white, decorated it with Coptic crosses, and altered the structure for occupation. Tomb 1448 was filled with straw and water vessels, apparently having been reused in Late Antique times as a stable. In tomb 1126 a potter's kiln was found, along with lamps and wine amphoras. This set of structures to the north and east of the village seems to have been the most conducive to temporary reoccupation and habitation, in contrast to the houses within the enclosure. Although still small in scale, Late Antique occupation of the site was thus more domestic in character than any since the village was abandoned at the end of the New Kingdom. Though Late Antique material is found in many tombs, discrete burials were only discovered within the Christianized temple precinct, datable to the sixth or seventh century A.D. Bruyere recorded a total of nine elaborately wrapped bodies from this period, which he presumed to be monks. It is possible that other individuals were buried within the precinct walls, since Bruyere suggested that the Christian cemetery extended further to the north-east toward the temenos. Nonfunerary usage appears to have been low-density and concentrated around the temple, which remained the focal point of the site throughout the Graeco-Roman and Late Antique periods.
The third category of subsequent activity, highdensity reuse and remodeling, is most telling in terms of levels of tomb reuse and reconstruction as well as burial practices. This last category is perhaps most pertinent to the decreasing focus upon the burial assemblage and increasing concentration on the body. Numerous tombs in the Western Necropolis housed great numbers of bodies dating from the Third Intermediate period to Graeco-Roman times; Christian burials do not seem to have been located in this part of the site. Bruyere did not record exact numbers of individuals, in part because of the great disturbance of the burials with consequential disarticulation of the bodies, but also because of his own lesser interest in the material. Moreover, anyone who has excavated tombs reused over a long period will appreciate the difficulties of making sense of the mass of debris. For example, tombs 1059, 1060, 1138, 1140, 1197, 1344A, and 1447 were recorded as containing Late-period individuals among the vestiges of earlier New Kingdom assemblages and human remains. In the Ptolemaic period numerous bodies were deposited in tombs 1126, 1233, and 1346, and in later times into 1126, 1140, 1153, 1154, and 1155.7- Datable Roman mummies appear in tombs 1332A and B and 1447, where there is a catacomb containing at least 60 Roman mummies, some with high-quality masks and shrouds, including a significant number of females and children. Post-New Kingdom burials include increased numbers of women and children whose burials were generally closer in elaboration and expense to their male counterparts than was the case in earlier times. This trend began in the Ramesside period and culminated in Graeco-Roman times. The burials of children are particularly conspicuous since they were copiously wrapped and gilded, in as elaborate a manner as adults. There is no evidence of comparable treatment of children from New Kingdom Deir el Medina. This democratization of burial is significant.
None of the tombs used in the Graeco-Roman period appears to have been constructed at the time of deposition; this reuse of tombs with mixed tomb assemblages and bodies suggests a certain disregard for the actual context of the burial itself. In New Kingdom times, the integrity of the tomb had been crucial. The mortuary cult of the deceased was enacted at the site of the tomb, and this had serious implications in afterlife scenarios. Baines and Lacovara have referred to the mortuary practices of pharaonic Egypt as forming a "mausoleum culture"; given the powerful associations of the tomb, this description is very apt. Tombs were constructed largely during the tomb owners' lifetime and as such were very much part of life-the superstructure being a visible and tangible reminder of one's death and the hereafter. In principle, the tomb formed a concrete, yet liminal, installation for maintaining the deceased in life and where the worlds of the living and the dead overlap. The preservation of the deceased's mummified body, the grave goods, and the integrity of the tomb itself were fundamental. The associated mortuary chapel was the locus for the mortuary cult, which was integral to the maintenance of the deceased. Lastly, there were spells and curses to protect against the desecration of the tomb.
Yet the primacy of the tomb structure was soon overturned after the New Kingdom, and the integrity and elaboration of the body itself became central. The practice of placing coffins in among the disarray of previous occupations further supports this reading. The lack of substantive burial assemblages that characterizes post-New Kingdom mortuary praxis suggests that it was not the paraphernalia but the body itself that became the single focus after death. This shift in focus may have begun toward the end of the New Kingdom, with the ever-dw associated tomb goods and a reduc personalized tombs. The materiality of death as well as its attendant material culture virtually disappeared, and the objectification of the body and bodily treatments took its place. As Baines and Lacovara remark, the mausoleum culture ultimately gave way to other concerns and modes of representation. From the emergence of the Egyptian state onward, "the preservation of the dead and their monuments was threatened by the passage of time and by competing concerns. By the end, it had become of relatively minor importance."
A number of interrelated points concerning temporal change, social inequality, and the history of the body can be derived from this analysis. Deir el Medina provides Egyptian archaeology with a rare opportunity to investigate issues such as the body, death, and sacred landscapes within the confines of a coherent data set. This study of diachronic funerary practices can only be undertaken because later social groups revered the site of Deir el Medina, from the Third Intermediate period to Late Antique times. While I have argued that there were residual social memories in terms of death and burial, these were not always historically embedded. The meanings layered upon the site were thus multiple and contingent through time.
First, in terms of material culture and funerary practices, there is observable diachronic change. During the 18th Dynasty the construction of the person in death resembles that of the living. This gradually shifts to a focus upon death and the afterlife in Ramesside times. In the New Kingdom these trends are reflected in the material constructions (tombs, chapels, shrines, tomb goods), preparations (mummification), practices (domestic, mortuary, and commemorative rituals), and beliefs (about the individual, death, afterlife, and cosmology). In the 18th Dynasty the tomb (its construction, decoration, funerary assemblage, and treatment of individual bodies) is constituted around the concept of the and all its earthly associations. In contrast, the situation for children appeared to be basically consistent across the social strata. The situation in the Ramesside period was markedly different. There is a move to generational tombs encompassing many individuals; while the visibility of women and children increases (hence the decline in Eastern Necropolis tombs), there is still a material discrepancy in favor of elite men and their male relatives. The increase in numbers of individuals present and the more favorable general treatment of women and children continue and peak in the Graeco-Roman period.
As I have argued elsewhere, the concept of embodiment links the physical, social, and psychical aspects of the individual. In Egypt, the body in death assumed different positions in specific contexts: it was subject during living experience and also object in the sphere of death. In the mortuary context, social practices and technologies transformed the living body into an elaborated dead, yet deified body. The individual became closer to the godly pharaonic body, and closer to the gods themselves. The beautiful death, linking mortals to pharaohs and gods, became of pivotal importance and continued to be enhanced, reaching its culmination in the hybrid culture of Graeco-Roman Egypt. In the latter period the cult of the body reached its apex, in life and death. Bodily practices, technologies, and ideologies become increasingly complex and articulated. The body has a long and fluid history at the site from the 18th Dynasty to Christian times, with a host of concomitant social ideologies woven around it. Concepts of the body changed radically and notions about individual bodies were linked to social axes of difference-age, sex, class, marital status, and wealth. The data from Deir el Medina are also informative in terms of bodily histories. I suggest that our knowledge of Egyptian death and burial is in fact construed from Ramesside (if not Late-period) information and that the material paraphernalia of death only became common-though not universal-at this time. For example, wealthy 18th Dynasty individuals such as Kha and Merit, and Sennefer and Nefertiry, were not mummified in spite of their apparent wealth. Moreover, the funerals of neonates, children, and adolescents in the Eastern Necropolis may not have conformed to the same practices as adults, though the emotional outlay may have been significant. There is no single Egyptian mortuary practice, and this material challenges the seemingly homogeneous picture set out in the documentary record. The experience of the Ramesside community was visibly different from that of the earlier 18th Dynasty community. They were a new population, some of whom had been alive through the Amarna upheaval, while others were indirectly affected by its aftermath. Assmann would propose that there were new sentiments about life, death, and piety, and more realizations about the contingencies of both worlds and the consequent fear of chaos. Alternatively, Baines argues that those sentiments were always prevalent, and it was simply a matter of being more able to represent this as an individual in Ramesside times. We need to consider Baines's question: was it a matter of reality or representation? The Ramesside period is known as the age of personal piety, and the villagers were noticeably vigilant in their religious duties. As Baines notes, if the gods were neglected, they might abandon humanity as they supposedly had during the Amarna period. Maintaining order was always fundamental in Egyptian culture and we can speculate that Ramesside people experienced tensions between the fear of chaos and instigating order. This may have translated into the bodily sphere. As a way of coping with contingency and controlling destiny, the body and the good death may have become central. People needed to perform elaborate rituals so that mortals could become gods in death, literally becoming an Osiris. This recognition must have had profound effects in the living sphere, prompting people to reflect on their life experiences, perhaps in a rather melancholic way. The experience of the Amarna period allowed all these aspects to be accommodated more fully in an ideological discourse, rather than being implicitly new phenomena. The people of Deir el Medina presumably oscillated between feelings of hedonism and fatalism--contradictory responses that were sometimes juxtaposed. Such moral uncertainties and worries were reflected in the New Kingdom Harper's songs8' inscribed in private tombs: they combine skepticism, hedonism, and piety. They best sum up the contradictions of an ancient society that, to our eyes, appears to have been fascinated with death and the hereafter, but in reality was obsessed with sustaining life beyond the liminal boundaries of death.

Predynastic and Early Dynastic Egypt:
Natural Mummies, Burial Customs and the Beginnings of a Cult of the Dead Verifiable remains of settlements of prehistoric cultures in Egypt go back as far as the 6th millennium BC. The most common burial position of a body in prehistoric times was the flexed pose (fig. 1): the body lay, wrapped in matting, in a shallow grave, with burial objects placed next to it. At first, the body was laid with the head pointing west, as a rule, but over time an eastward orientation predominated. The civilizations based in Upper Egypt buried their dead in desert areas bordering villages, where the body was exposed to sun and salty desert sand, which led to preservation through desiccation. Today it is assumed that this effect caused by the environment made its mark on the religious concept of a death cult, which took physical preservation as a necessary condition for the afterlife. With the formation of the first population centres and elite cemeteries, in c. 3700 BC, there was a change in grave structures. Grave pits became larger and their walls were partially sealed with bricks, which may have protected the bodies from sun and sand, but which also hindered natural mummification. For a long time, received opinion in Egyptology held that the decomposition observed from altered burial conditions was the only impetus for the development of artificial mummification. This would be because, once the establishment of a cult of the dead was fixed, a corpse had to be protected from decay at all costs. Following the latest finds in a workers’ cemetery in Hierakonpolis (HK 43), dating from c. 3600 BC, however, it seems that other concepts of the afterlife were already playing a role: the bodies of The term “mummy” is understood in the natural sciences to be a preserved human or animal corpse, including skin, hair, and flesh, regardless of whether it has been created by natural processes or by artificial methods. In addition, in Egyptology, a wrapped body is also usually referred to as a mummy when the silhouette of the dead person has been preserved, yet only skeletal remains are found within the wrappings. The next step in mummification practice was typified by the mummy of a civilian, Ranefer (Fourth or Fifth Dynasty, c. 2500 BC), who was discovered in Meidum, his organs wrapped in linen and stored in a niche next to his body. Ranefer’s linen-wrapped head (fig. 3) had eyes, eyebrows, hair and a mouth painted on it, and the shapes of his body parts had been reproduced, his facial features being modeled with particular care. In what had become common practice, the embalmers had completely wrapped the body in resin-soaked cloths and bandages. In addition—and also a new procedure—the abdomen had been stuffed with resin-soaked linen. This mummy, housed in the Royal College of Surgeons in London and destroyed during World War II, is a clear indication that the Egyptians of Ranefer’s time attached great importance to the systematic treatment of the outer wrappings, a tradition which lasted initially until the end of the Old Kingdom, as evidenced by other mummies of this type from Saqqara, Giza and Abusir. The parts of the human body, including the genitals, were reconstructed with the aid of linen bandages and resin. Towards the end of the Old Kingdom, separate cartonnage funerary masks appeared, which, from then on were a distinguishing feature of Egyptian mummies, especially during the far back in early Egyptian history, perhaps over 1,000 years, earlier ideas existed that considered reuniting limbs separated by death. At any rate, skeletons with signs of decapitation and dismemberment occurred only sporadically, and then mainly in non-elite circles. During the preparation of the dead in later eras, the restoration of an intact body, which was supposed to be produced by bandaging and embalming, among other things, was of considerable importance. The Old Kingdom: Removal of Internal Organs and Arrangement of Outer Wrappings The Third Dynasty (c. 2700 BC) ushered in the first peak of Egyptian civilization (Third to Sixth Dynasties, c. 2700–2200 BC): the Old Kingdom, which is characterized by great architectural monuments of stone, above all, the pyramids.
The most important evidence for a chronology of mummification techniques came from royal settings. Around 2600 BC, the removal of internal organs (evisceration) became common procedure for people, such as relatives and high officials, buried in the royal residence cemeteries. This suppressed the process of decomposition. At the beginning of the Fourth Dynasty there is only indirect proof of evisceration, in the form of niches in grave walls, each with four compartments. The compartments may have contained four organs: the stomach, intestines, lungs and liver, as this treatment was applied in later eras, when canopic jars, special containers for inner organs, or chests, were used. The earliest evidence of a canopic container was found in the tomb of Hetepheres I, mother of Khufu, whose linen-wrapped viscera were kept in an alabaster chest with four compartments. A fluid adhering to the linen proved to be a 3% natron solution—a rare early instance of the application of natron, which was not used extensively in mummification until the Middle Kingdom. The tomb of Meresanch III, granddaughter of Khufu and wife of Khafra, yields the oldest evidence for the preservation of organs in four canopic jars, which, in turn, were placed in a canopic chest. Although inner organs were occasionally removed at this time, there is still no evidence of the extraction of the brain on a regular basis during the Old Kingdom. A few individual cases perhaps indicate an experimental phase. Once removal of the inner organs became part of the process, bodies were laid out on their backs for burial. 3 Mummified head of Ranefer, c. 2500 BC.
The picture of how the dead were handled during the pre- and protohistoric eras is very incomplete. A few bodies (in El Adaima, Hierankonpolis, Naqada, but also later, during the Old Kingdom, in Giza, Meidum, and Deshasha) were dismembered, or had skin and muscle tissue removed from their bones, long before burial but certainly after death. Other bodies show the first signs of the application of mummification techniques. The enormous importance of the body’s transitional period from time of death to burial is evident in the various forms of body treatment. A general explanation for the dismemberment of the bodies continues to be the subject of heated debate (Dougherty and Friedman 2008).
It is not until the following era, in the ritual texts of the dead, that a written description of the concepts connected to dismemberment exist, such as this excerpt from a text from the pyramid of Teti (PT 413; §§ 735b–736c): “Awake, O King, raise yourself, receive your head, gather your bones together, shake off your dust, and sit on your iron throne, so that you may eat the foreleg, devour the haunch, and partake of your ribjoints in the sky in company with the gods.”1 These so-called Pyramid Texts, which first appear during the reign of Unas, the last ruler of the Fifth Dynasty, are the oldest written records from which the Egyptian concept of the afterlife is known. The over 700 individual spells give an incongruous, sometimes even contradictory, picture. It is not possible to say how three prominent women of the time were found, covered with mats, with their necks and hands wrapped in fine linen soaked in resin—a measure which, compared to exposure to sun and sand, was not conducive to greater preservation of soft tissues. One of the women had had her throat cut after her death; another woman had an organ removed, which was then wrapped in a resin-soaked cloth and put back in her body (fig. 1). It is possible to speculate as to why this was done. It appears that the most important priority was not the long-term appearance of the body, but rather the preservation of particular body functions. Therefore, those parts of the body that were necessary for the consumption of food were together and could not be lost. Linen soaked in resin has also been found in the graves of the oldest protohistoric burial sites, such as Mostagedda (c. 4000 BC). If the goal of postmortem manipulation was “mummification”, in the sense of preservation of soft tissues, even if in the beginning it was only specific tissues, this can be seen as evidence of the beginnings of artificial preservation of bodies going back as far as 6,000 years. The goal itself, as shown by the finds, had not yet been reached. The creation and development of a unified state in Egypt took place through a long process (0 Dynasty) around the year 3000 BC. Resin-soaked linen bandages, such as were known early in history, were found with skeletal remains in the necropolises of the 1st and 2nd dynasties (c. 3050–2700 BC) in Saqqara and Abydos. The better-preserved burials in Saqqara show bodies in flexed pose, wrapped in heavy layers of linen and buried in wooden coffins. Their soft tissues are also not preserved. The bodies found in the royal tombs of Abydos have only a few impregnated linen cloths with pieces of bone clinging to them. They come from the Dewen tomb area and were originally assigned to the royal graves of Djer, Djet, Dewen and Merneith. What is probably the best-known fragment was found by a member of Petrie’s excavation team in 1901 in the tomb complex of King Djer (c. 3000 BC): a lower arm, wrapped in fine linen and wearing four bracelets made of gold, turquoise, lapis lazuli and amethyst. Preservation of the skin or muscle tissues had not occurred (fig. 2). It is generally accepted that the arm was that of Djer or his wife, Merneith. At the beginning of the 20th century no particular importance was attached to the find; the curator of the Cairo museum at the time is said to have thrown away the bandages along with the arm. The bracelets are still on display in the museum. 2 The linen-wrapped lower arm of King Djer or his consort Merneith, Abydos, c. 3000 BC.
The practice of using coffins and wrapping the body spread to provincial cemeteries, even for simpler burials. The kingdom was not reunited until about a century later, under the rule of Upper Egypt (Middle Kingdom, c. 2100–1790 BC), yet there were still autonomous local rulers who no longer had themselves buried near the king—as was still usually the case for upper officials in the previous era—but who built their own necropolises. Mummification techniques were accordingly diverse, probably due in part to different financial means, but nonetheless a further development was observed in individual cases. Cartonnage masks, which had appeared at the end of the Sixth Dynasty, were now found on a majority of mummies. During the reign of Mentuhotep II (c. 2000 BC) this developed into the anthropoid coffin type, which housed mummies of especially high-ranking individuals. Particular importance was still given to the outer appearance of the dead body: considerable amounts of linen cloth were used for wrapping. Body parts were not only wrapped individually and bandaged together to form the typical mummy shape; the finished mummy was then sometimes wrapped in more layers of linen which formed a sort of cocoon. An example of this can be seen in the mummy of Wah from the Eleventh Dynasty, found in Thebes (fig. 6). Amulets providing protection were placed in the layers of linen. As in the Old Kingdom, the linen was sometimes partially coated with resin. Since the resin was not applied directly to the skin, however, its fungicidal and bactericidal properties did not aid the preservation process, if this, indeed, was its intended purpose. Natron was the most important means of preserving soft tissues since the Middle Kingdom. The removal of not only of viscera, but also now of the contents of the skull, in some cases, was also helpful in preventing decomposition. This was practiced rarely and was presumably a privilege of the wealthier classes (Strouhal 1986). In the New Kingdom, from c. 1550 BC, transnasal brain removal became more common: an approximately 30 cm (11.8 in) long hooked metal rod was inserted, as a rule, through the left nostril, perforating the ethmoid bone (lamina cribrosa). The hook was then used to crush the brain, which was then removed through the nose. The viscera were removed, as in the Old Kingdom, through the abdominal wall; the left side was usually cut open. From the Twelfth Dynasty (c. 1990 BC) onwards, heated resin was applied directly to the skin, a treatment which could be seen in individual cases as early as in the Old Kingdom.

Through the help of embalming and mummification rites, a person was reconstructed, reintegrated and conveyed in a living form, so that he would be able to enter into another realm of life (heaven, underworld, or the earth’s interior).
The First Intermediate Period and Middle Kingdom: A Combination of Techniques to Prevent Decomposition The First Intermediate Period (c. 2200 BC) saw the collapse of a central authority; local rulers gained power. 5 Ba and shadow, from the tomb of Irinefer, west of Thebes (TT 290), c. 1250 BC.
were made to preserve the soft tissues: “O flesh of Teti, rot not, decay not, stink not.” (PT §722). Any decomposition, violation or neglect of the corpse would extinguish the person once and for all. The body, therefore, had to be supplied regularly with food. This could be done by magic, through images or sacrificial texts, and the tomb had to be maintained accordingly, in order to function as the meeting place for the transfigured dead and the living.
For life in the afterworld, which was supposed to be comparable to life in the earthly world, three constituents which made up a person were of great importance: Ba, Ka, and Akh. The Ba established the connection with the dead body. It became separated from the body at death, was able to fly in the form of a bird between this world and the next, and always returned to the body (fig. 5). Ka was the concept of a moral character, a person’s double, to which social categories such as honor, dignity and status were tied. After death, Ka separated from the body and was able to confront the deceased. Akh was the spirit of the transfigured dead person. One of the aims of the funerary rites was to carry the dead person across in his Akh Middle Kingdom and the Greco-Roman periods. Full body coverings, made of several layers of plaster with care-fully reconstructed facial features (fig. 4), which were fitted onto the bandaged contours of the body were common in the Fifth and Sixth Dynasties (c. 2500–2200 BC). Although this esthetic covering did nothing to protect against decomposition, it nevertheless restored to the body its individual shape and functionality, which were considered necessary for an existence in the afterlife.
No intact royal mummies have survived from the Old Kingdom, but there are individual body parts that can be attributed to that time, due to their discovery location and carbon-14 dating. Examples include the mummified hand of Neferefre (c. 2450 BC) and the remains of Djedkare-Isesi (c. 2400 BC), two kings of the Fifth Dynasty. The skeletal remains, including a foot wrapped in linen, which were for a long time attributed to Djoser, the most important king of the Third Dynasty, have now been radiocarbon dated to the Ptolemaic era. Belief in the Afterworld Towards the end of the Old Kingdom, a concept of the afterworld was established and became dominant until the end of Egyptian civilization, and even beyond. Just as the dead kings had earlier experienced the fate of the god Osiris, so did the non-royal dead as well. In mythology at first only alluded to, Osiris was the ruler of Egypt as successor to his father, Geb, and was killed by his brother and rival for the royal throne, Seth. Seth dismembered his victim and scattered his limbs throughout the land, but Osiris’s sisters, Isis and Nephthys, searched for the body parts and put their brother’s body back together. In the course of this archtypical mummification Osiris was not only resurrected; he also fathered a son by Isis, Horus, who avenged his father’s killing and became the new ruler of Egypt. From this time on, Osiris was king and commander of the afterworld.
As a result of this, the deceased person, upon his burial, received a so-called Osiris name, which would identify him to the lord of the afterworld and thus allow his existence in the afterlife. This magical language complemented the older mummification theories but did not replace them; the meticulous preservation of bodies and the care given to the buried continued to be regarded as essential for their continued existence. Missing body parts were restored or replaced. The state of mummification technology during the New Kingdom can be reconstructed, thanks to the preservation of these mummies, although not every pharaoh benefited from all the various treatments. Transnasal brain removal became standard practice. Resin was applied generously, not only directly on the skin, but also poured through the nose into the brain. It was also used in the form of plugs inserted into the nasal and aural orifices, occasionally also into the anus, and served as a glue to seal the incision made into the left side of the abdomen, which was then covered by a sheet of gold. The heart always remained in the body, sometimes receiving its own linen wrappings. After removal of the organs, body cavities were cleansed with water and wine, and then stuffed with natron, resin, and/or linen. After drying, embalming and wrapping, the organs were placed in canopic jars. Particularly during the late New Kingdom, these containers sometimes had lids decorated with the characteristic heads of the four sons of Horus: Amset with a human head, Hapi with a baboon head, Duamutef with a jackal head, and Qebehsenuef with a falcon head (fig. 9). After the cleansing and drying phases, which started four days after death and lasted about 48 days, and the adornment of the outer appearance through artificial hair extensions, hair dyeing, blackened eyebrows, and other aesthetic modifications, the mummy was wrapped from head to foot, during which amulets were distributed between the linen bandages, and given its shape by stuffing its body cavities. The body was then placed in the coffin and, in some cases, then covered with a layer of resin. Embalming and wrapping took about 14 days, while seventy days were ideally needed for the entire process. The drying agents, ointments and linen cloths that were used, along with the remains of hair and nails from the embalmed body, were stored separately in containers or coffins and buried near the mummy’s tomb. Mummies found in unplundered tombs are especially noteworthy. A remarkable example is Senebtisi from Lisht (Twelfth Dynasty). Her body was laid on her left side, as was typical during the Middle Kingdom, with her face pointing east. Her inner organs were removed through an incision on the left side of her abdomen; her heart, wrapped in linen, was replaced in its correct position in the body, and the abdominal cavity was then stuffed with resin-soaked cloth and sealed with resin. The brain was left in the skull. Senebitsi’s mummy in its anthropoid coffin was then covered with such a large quantity of pitch that its considerable remains are still visible on the body and in the coffin (fig. 7). None of the royal mummies from the Middle Kingdom has been preserved. The mummies of six ladies from the royal family of the Eleventh Dynasty, however, were found in shaft graves behind the temple complex of Mentuhotep-Nebhepetre in Deir el-Bahri. Rather surprising, in view of their social status, was the fact that neither the viscera nor the brain were removed. Nonetheless, they were in a good state of preservation; mummification had taken place due to the use of natron, along with resin and beeswax.
Customarily, after the organs were removed the empty abdominal cavity was filled with linen; sawdust was also sometimes used. After removal the inner organs were stored in four canopic jars, while the brain, which was regarded as unimportant (the heart being considered the seat of the mind), was discarded. The shape of the jars changed during the course of Egyptian history, but there were always four of them. From the First Intermediate Period onwards the lids sometimes featured human heads, and starting with the Middle Kingdom the containers display inscriptions putting them under the protection of the four sons of Horus: Amset, Hapi, Qebehsenuef and Duamutef. On occasion, tombs with canopic jars were found, although the internal organs were still in the body. The jars, therefore, had a significance far greater than that of being simple containers for holding the stomach, intestines, liver and lungs.

In the New Kingdom, as a rule, any missing body parts were reconstructed and replaced during the mummification process with the aid of bandages, resin or wood. Mummification was not only a privilege of the elite in Pharaonic Egypt; persons of non-royal lineage were also embalmed for the voyage to the afterworld, albeit with less elaborate techniques: there was no evisceration, but the body was probably desiccated by the use of natron, then treated with resin and wrapped in linen bandages.
The Third Intermediate Period: The Use of Padding Under the Skin Today, it is often stressed that the art of embalming reached its pinnacle during the Twenty-First Dynasty, around 1000 BC. At that time, many royal bodies were moved to the cachettes, which made it possible for embalmers to notice any technical faults when viewing the mummies of previous generations that had fallen victim to tomb robbers. At any rate, this period witnessed a conspicuous change in techniques. The skin was cut open on many places of the dead body, and the inner surface lined with sawdust, linen, resin or mud, in order for the body to retain its shape despite desiccation (fig. 8f). Since, in some cases, onions were also wrapped onto other parts of the body and were identified with the teeth of Osiris as far back as the Pyramid Texts, and in addition during the New Kingdom onions played an important role as a cult object in a feast celebrating the regeneration of the mummified Sokar-Osiris, their use was not, or not only, due to their anti-bacterial properties, as has been assumed.
In some cases the bandages were applied with particular care. The mummy of Ramses II is a good example: small animal bones were used to bandage his nose in such a way that the nostrils remained open. Great importance was given to the nose in the Egyptian imagination, since this was where the breath of life entered the body. This is why the act of smashing the nose from a statue of the deceased person was a very serious punishment, since the victim would be denied an existence in the afterlife. In a few cases, excessive padding resulted in an unnatural appearance or in the skin bursting open, although the intention must certainly have been to create a natural image: the head and body were painted in the colors made familiar from paintings and statues— red for a man, yellow for a woman. With the advent of the Twenty-First Dynasty, burial of the inner organs outside the body fell out of use, possibly as a result of previous tomb robbing. From this point on, the organs which were removed through the side of the abdomen were placed back in the body, often together with the wax figures of the protective deities. During this time the brain continued to be removed through the nose. The skull and body cavities were filled with melted resin. By the Twenty-Second Dynasty (c. 950 BC), the use of direct body preparation, such as shaping the body underneath the skin, declined in favor of a return to shaping the outer hull through additional linen. The preservation of soft tissue may also have been less important, although based on evidence this cannot be demonstrated convincingly. Given that there are no royal mummies preserved either from the Late Period (746–332 BC) or the Ptolemaic Dynasty (332–330 BC), it appears that the current scientifically-held view that the knowledge of mummification collapsed completely at that time is much too sweeping. Differences in the practice of mummification according to social status can clearly be recognized up to the Roman period. The Late Period: The Greek Historian Herodotus describes the Art of Embalming During the Twenty-Fifth Dynasty it became common to place the inner organs between the thighs or calves after their embalming; the canopic jars also found in such tombs had a purely symbolic function. The majority of Late Period mummies come from Upper Egypt and the areas bordering it (see Budde article in this volume). A tomb site in el-Assasif (Thebes) was especially rich in finds: in the funerary chamber of Wahibre a complete set of copper embalming instruments was discovered. It contained a knife, an enema device (still encrusted with brown and white matter), a spatula, tweezers, a spoon, a needle, and a hook. As in earlier times, the preparation of the mummy depended on social status and monetary resources. Herodotus of Helicarnassus (c. 484–425 BC) wrote in his Histories (II, 85–8) that at the time of Persian rule there existed several methods of mummification, according to means:
“Thus do they embalm according to the best of these ways:—First with a crooked iron tool they draw out the brain through the nostrils, extracting it partly thus and partly by pouring in drugs; and after this with a sharp stone of Ethiopia they make a cut along the side and take out the whole contents of the belly, and when they have cleared out the cavity and cleansed it with palmwine they cleanse it again with spices pounded up: then they fill the belly with pure myrrh pounded up and with cassia and other spices except frankincense, and sew it together again. The Greco-Roman Period: Individualized Mummies and Refined Bandaging Technique The bodies embalmed for the afterlife in Ptolemaic and Roman Egypt (332 BC–395 AD) today present a disparate picture of varying techniques and local customs, not only in their outward appearence, but also as far as organ preservation is concerned. Great importance continued to be given to the outer appearance of mummies. A large number of variations were noted from among the mummies found in the “Valley of the Golden Mummies”. This necropolis, which was discovered quite recently, in 1996, in the Bahariya Oasis, holds 105 intact mummies just in the area excavated so far. They date back to the first century AD. The bodies of the elite were completely and meticulously bandaged with strips of linen, and their heads and chests were covered by cartonnage masks which were painted and, on 60 of the masks, gilded. The gods on the breastplates and the depictions of scenes from the Egyptian Book of the Dead show that the old beliefs about the afterworld were still widespread, although the masks, with their contemporary hairstyles, headgear and facial expressions, were fashioned in the Roman style. It was probably primarily members of the middle class who were bandaged in linen, but had to do without masks, painting and gold. The bandaging was done extremely carefully to produce a geometric pattern (criss-cross pattern). By contrast, the poorest Oasis inhabitants were rather carelessly bandaged, so that in a few cases the bandages have fallen apart over time. Extensive analysis of the preservation methods in the Bahariya mummies have yet to be carried out, but data from other excavations provide some relevant information. The anthropological investigation of bodies from the Douch necropolis (end of the Ptolemaic era until the mid-5th century AD) in the Kharga Oasis has revealed that various methods were employed to prevent decomposition, apparently depending on the status of the deceased. In the most elaborate type of burial, which can be distinguished superficially by the traces of gold on the face, hands, and feet, the brain and abdomen were emptied and the skull was filled with embalming material. In a second group of mummies, the brains were missing, although the bodies contained all of their viscera; the skin on the bodies was anointed with embalming agents. The mummies of a third type were not chemically treated and the interior of the and protective rites at the tomb. The Embalming Ritual Egyptian text sources do not describe the methods used for cleaning and drying the corpse. The techniques of wrapping and embalming, on the other hand, are found in the so-called embalming ritual, which is Natron was used as a desiccant in mummification. Chemically speaking, this was not lye—which some modern translations of the word borrowed by the Greeks and used in Herodotus would have us think—but a mixture of sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate, together with smaller amounts of sodium chloride and sodium sulfate, such as was collected by the ancient Egyptians, mainly on the shores of Wadi el Natrun Lake. The desiccating effect comes mainly from the crystallized sodium carbonate, to which up to 10% water can bind without appearing wet. Dehydration could be hastened by repeatedly replacing the layers of salt; wood shavings and linen also supported the process. After dehydration the body was treated with ointments and resins, sometimes also bitumen. An Egyptian word for “bitumen” was not encountered until the New Kingdom, but the substance was probably already known through trade relations with Mesopotamia. There, it was employed to seal structures against water, a use the Egyptians noticed and adapted for the purpose of embalming corpses. The relatively late appearance (during the Twentieth Dynasty) of an Egyptian word for bitumen is matched by archaeological finds. Analysis of mummies shows the first evidence of bitumen in the 9th century BC (Twenty-Second Dynasty); at that time it was extracted from natural deposits at Gebel Zeit (Mons Petrolius) and Abu Durba on the shores of the Gulf of Suez. In the Greco-Roman period mummies were also treated with bitumen from the Dead Sea, which is confirmed not only by analysis, but by Greek writings. Diodorus Siculus (19.9) mentions the bitumen of the Dead Sea thus: “The barbarians who enjoy this source of income take the asphalt to Egypt and sell it for the embalming of the dead; for unless this is mixed with the other aromatic ingredients, the preservation of the bodies cannot be permanent.”6 Posidonios similarly remarks in Strabo (16.2): “The Egyptians use the asphalt for the embalming of their dead.”7 Like resin and beeswax, the black-brown substance softened when heated and was used alone or in combination with other salve ingredients—there is evidence of blending with animal and vegetable oils. Due to its liquid-repellant properties, bitumen protected natron-dried bodies from rehydration and subsequent decomposition.
Beeswax had a similar effect and was used in mummification from the Middle Kingdom. Beeswax was not mentioned as an embalming agent in medieval or early modern texts, but in Egyptian embalming texts embalms ... In Egypt, indeed, the corpse, duly dried, is actually placed at table—I have seen it done.”4 And Saint Anthony, an Egyptian monk, was afraid he might not receive the burial due to a pious Christian, according to Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria (c. 298–373): “if you have any care for me and are mindful of me as of a father, suffer no one to take my body into Egypt, lest haply they place me in the houses.”5 The End of Mummification With the Edict of Theodosius in 392 AD, all “heathen” cults were prohibited. The practice of mummification, however, did not fall under the ban, since Coptic Christians continued occasionally to preserve the bodies of especially venerated persons by the use of salt (without, however, evisceration), then storing and taking care of them (fig. 14). In Christianity, and related cultures, the corpse as a companion of the living has never become obsolete, as exemplified by Lenin’s mummy (whose brain was removed for “scientific” investigation) and the Capuchin catacombs of Palermo,; as well as the highly complex Christian cult of relics. In Egypt, meanwhile, the expansion of Islam in 641 AD put an abrupt end to the religious importance of the human corpse. According to Muslim rite, if a person dies in the morning he is buried on the same day, otherwise burial is on the next day. The body—unpreserved, but washed and wrapped in white cloth—is given to the earth of Europe, which destroys, or to the sand of the desert, which still desiccates; respect for the peace of the deceased is so great that almost any type of ornament or maintenance for the grave is dispensed with, at least in the case of ordinary mortals. Appendix: The Most Important Embalming Agents Evidence for the agents used in embalming is found in ancient texts as well as in the material remaining on mummies and vessels. Analyzing the text sources, such as from the above-quoted embalming ritual, the ritual book for the embalming of the Apis bulls, the accounts from embalming workshops, and the inscriptions from vessels found in embalming caches, is problematic, since the ingredients that are named cannot all be identified with certainty. Only the substances natron, asphalt, wax, pitch, and myrrh can be safely translated from their historic meaning.
Certain visible features are typical in mummies of the Greco-Roman period. First, a refinement of bandaging techniques was noted (fig. 13). Plaster masks on mummies, mainly from Hermopolis in Middle Egypt, have been preserved. A distinctive feature that originated in Egypt during Roman domination (1st –3rd centuries AD) are the so-called portrait mummies, a large number of which have been found in the necropolises of the Faiyum Oasis, Antinopolis, and Akhmim. The mummies were carefully wrapped and their faces are overlaid with a thin wooden board bearing a portrait of the face of the deceased painted in encaustic or tempera technique (figs. 12, 13). The oldest known mummies of this type come from the reign of the emperor Tiberius (14–37 AD), the most recent from the 4th century AD.
The main motive for the introduction of portraits into the cult of the dead is considered to be the everincreasing desire for overt self-portrayal. The deceased was no longer idealized, but personalized, although he continued to identify himself with Osiris. Members of the Roman elite living in Egypt were able to adopt Egyptian concepts of the afterlife, as proven by images of funerary art.
There is also a visible change to burial practices. Sometimes, apparently, years could pass between death and burial, during which time the mummified person would remain in the house of his or her surviving family. The Greek-writing satirist Lucian of Samosata (c. 120–after 180 AD), who spent several years in Egypt, described it (De luctu 21): “the Egyptian 14 Female mummy from Antinopolis from the 4th century AD, natural mummification. The human remains from the necropolis at Kellis (end of Ptolemaic era to 400 AD) in the Dakhla Oasis can also be differentiated according to their mummification status: some of the bodies are natural mummies, while others have been preserved through human intervention. In total, 94% of these bodies had their brains removed transnasally; in contrast to the Kharga mummies, however, no embalming liquids had been poured into the skull. In some of the deceased, the inner organs were removed through an incision in the left side of the body or through the rectum, and the body cavities were filled with embalming matter and resin-soaked balls of linen. In addition, hot resin had been applied to the skin—in some cases, this was the only action taken. There is no evidence that natron had been used to dry out the corpse.
It is also known from tombs in the Nile Valley that the methods used often varied. Evisceration was encountered less in mummies from the Greco-Roman period, and the use of natron seems to have ceased completely. All the more conspicuous is the generous use of embalming agents, which were applied in the body’s cavities as well as on its surface. In those cases where the brain had been removed, this was done either in the traditional way, through the ethmoid bone (lamina cribrosa) and the nasal cavity, or in a simpler way, through the large hole at the bottom of the skull (foramen magnum).

Rich., and also species of juniper, such as Juniperus oxycedrus L., the question arose as to whether it was cedar resin or oil of juniper (juniper species do not yield resin, but instead an essential oil) that was used as an embalming agent. Analysis speaks convincingly in favor of cedar, however; it is important to note that traces of Aleppo pine resin have also been found in mummies dating back as far as the Twenty-Third Dynasty, as has pistachio resin from Pistacia lentiscus L.
Among the embalming agents mentioned by Herodotus and Diodorus was a substance that, so far, has not been found through analysis: cinnamon. The fact that it was named as a scent, plus the lack of any surviving traces of it, indicate that cinnamon was not used as a solid substance, but rather as a scented oil, whose delicate components have long since evaporated. Cinnamon—the cassia of which Herodotus spoke, is now thought to be “China” cinnamon, while the cinnamomum mentioned by Diodorus is “Ceylon” cinnamon. It was apparently a very unusual ingredient, originating as it did in faraway regions. There is, at present, no archaeological evidence for its importation into Egypt. Myrrh also had to be imported, and was also counted among the most precious of ingredients. Today, the source plant of myrrh for pharmaceutical uses is considered to be Commiphora molmol (Engl.), but the resin from other species of Commiphora (family Burseraceae) is also referred to as myrrh. This liquid gum resin, which seeps out of cracks in the tree bark and hardens on contact with air, gives off a faint, aromatic odor and has a lingering bitter taste. In the countries where it is collected it is separated into different grades of quality, according to its composition, so that imported resin may consist of a mixture of resin coming from different source plants. The genus Commiphora comprises over two hundred species and grows from the Red Sea to South Africa, and in India. Just as we can hardly determine the origin of individual resins today, so must we also accept that the term “myrrh resin” in antiquity has a very wide-ranging meaning.

Since Egypt was poor in resin-rich tree species, the embalming agent had to be imported. Starting in the Eighteenth Dynasty, resin from cedars (Cedrus atlantica (Endl.) Manetti) was used in mummification. Depending on the particular type of resin available from traders at the time, whether resinous wood or lumps of dried resin, various techniques were needed to prepare the embalming substance. A viscous, spreadable preparation was obtained by warming the resin, but heating it a high temperature under airtight conditions created pitch. Some texts actually refer to it as a “hot drug”. Shrouds from the Roman period also feature the jackalheaded Anubis, the god of the dead responsible for embalming, in his role as preparer of ointments, cooking the mummification substance on a stove (fig. 15). The anti-bacterial and antifungal properties of wood tars have long been known, but a more recent discovery is that some of the components they contain, principally guaiacol and other phenols, have such potent preservative qualities that an alkaline bone enzyme found in Egyptian mummies is still immunologically and enzymatically active, even today.
Both Herodotus and Diodorus mention “kedros” as an embalming agent. Pliny (XXIV, [21] 52), writing about kedros, says that it was the name for liquid pitch in Syria, and that it in Europe it is prepared from the Arolla pine. He described a method of extracting pitch from wood which is rich in resin. For a long time it was debated as to exactly which resin kedros referred; as a rule, the kedros of Herodotus and Diodorus is translated as “cedar resin”. Since Paleolithic man believed in an afterlife and even in Mesoamerica and the Andes cultures, care and ceremony were practiced to the burial of the dead in an ancestral cult. Introduction The Ancient and New World are full of examples of burial customs, preserving the dead in a natural or artificial form. Although mummified human remains have been found in almost all continents, especially in six principal regions, few people introduced this technique responding to religious purposes, ancestral cult or a belief in the dead powers. In the New World, we can mention the Andean cultures in the Pre-Hispanic America, Aluet people near Alaska, in the North Pacific Ocean, including Torres Strait Islander groups of the coastal areas of north-east Australia, and in the Ancient World the Egyptians in Africa and certain Buddhist priests of Japan in Asia . They performed autopsies and studied the human and animal anatomy comparatively. After evisceration, the central cavity was stuffed with dried grass. They next put the body into a running stream to dissolve the fat, leaving merely muscle and skin, tied in a flexed position, the corpse was dried by exposing to the air for a long period or occasionaly to fire. During this process his spirit could be ‘sealed in’ to a family member’s body. Once completed the drying, the deceased was wrapped in fur, mats or bird skins to rest in a wooden or rock shelf-like platform inside a cave. In this paper, we will only study two of these cultures, the Andean tradition, especially Chinchorro, and the Egyptian position in order to determine where this intentional technique took place first.
Since Paleolithic, man buried the dead according to elaborate conventions as an ancestral cult and even in Mesoamerica and the Andean cultures, evidence of belief in the afterlife appears. In Predynastic Egypt (4500-3100 BC), funerary customs were practised but apparently they had begun before in America, c. 5000 BC. We can also compare the cultivation extent in order to have an idea of the different processes in both worlds. In the case of agriculture, at the end of the Pleistocene, (c. 9500 BC) mixed foraging and cultivation strategies appeared in the Old World in the so-called Fertile Crescent.
But during the next pre-Pottery Neolithic, agro-pastoralism had replaced hunting and gathering through much of the Fertile Crescent (c. 9000-8000 BC). In the case of the New World, the items found recently in the Andes Mountains, in the intermontaneous region of Callejón of Huaylas, Ancash, Peru around 30 years ago, prove an earlier development, born independently of external influence. This archaeological site in Guitarrero Cave that contains human evidence of occupation, beginning approximately in 12,100 includes the earliest textiles identified in South America and stone tools.
It probably proves that the first agriculture in Peru is dated between 11,500-10,500 BC. In Tehuacan Valley, the early agricultural sites at Guila-Naquitz (8000 BC) evidence that Mexico began in a little later period than Guitarrero. Maybe this demonstrates that agriculture began earlier in the New World than in Egypt.
Agriculture and cemeteries in Egypt In the North, people migrations to the Nile began in the first Neolithic (c. 8000 BC) but around 5000 BC Neolithic settlements appeared all over Egypt. The Northern Merimde culture came about 5000 to 4200 BC, producing rudimentary ships that connected all the hamlets along the Nile River. Then, Fayum culture developed in 5000 BC and the first traces of cultivated plants were found there, near Cairo.
A new cycle began in 4000 BC, Omari age corresponding to Archaic Period; Buto Maadi cemeteries appeared at that time. They were not only herders and hunters but they also cultivated the land.
In the South, Upper Egypt, Badarian small groups of 40 to 100 people, gathered there from 4400 to 4000 BC, grew wheat and barley and created an irrigation system. Their practice of wrapping the dead body in animal skins spread during the Middle and Late Pre-dynastic periods (4500-3100 BC). At the same time in Northern Fayum A, Calcholite followed the Neolithic Tasian culture considered Stone Age. Amratian culture or Naqada I, very similar to Badarian, flourished between 4000-3500 BC and was followed by Gerzean culture or Naqada II (3500-3200 BC). It was largely an uninterrupted development of the first culture, starting in the Delta and moving to the South, establishing sedentary lifestyle. The first appearance of royal cemeteries, hieroglyphs, irrigation and first serek took place in Naqada III or Protodynastic period (3200-3000 BC).
Preserving the corps of dead Is the case of agriculture in America the same as mummification? Mummies may have served as a means of assisting the soul to survive and preventing the deceased from frightening the livings. A more commonly accepted theory is that there was an ancestor cult, delaying the final burial. Some evidence demonstrates that they travelled with the groups and took the place of honor during major rituals. The surprising perfection of Incan technique was achieved after other Andean cultures including their older predecessors, the Chinchorro culture, on the arid coast of the Atacama Desert between 7000-1500 BC. Frequently a basket or a leather pillow was placed over the head to insulate the face from the surrounding sand, as it was found in three children’s graves at Mostaggeda (4000 BC) in Upper Egypt. The corpse decomposition fluids, absorbed by the dryness of the desert, saved them from the complete decay and they soon became desiccated with well preserved skin and hair. The grave pit, itself, was not roofed over until considerably later and multiple room tombs, under the Mesopotamian influence, appeared in Naqada II.
This practice involved different aims in both worlds: natural desiccation, skin and flesh removal replaced by clay; black, red or mud-coated materials, evisceration, body cavity treatments, drying, cleansing and anointing the interior, brain removal, corpses covered with natron before being washed and wrapped. Mummification can also be described as externally prepared mummies (fig. 1), internally prepared mummies (Egyptian Pharaohs) (fig. 2) and reconstructed mummies (Chinchorro) (fig. 3).
Mummy chronologie and beliefs in America The cultural diversity of prehispanic America is unified regarding beliefs about the afterlife and the funeral ritual to become ancestors in a cyclical life.
Both the Mayan and Mesoamerican civilizations showed great interest in death. They believed that cosmos had three major planes: the Earth, the Heaven above, celestial paradise of heroic kings and warriors, and the Underworld Xibalba, translated ‘Place of Fear or Phantoms’. Structured in 9 levels below, reached by caves, cenotes and tunnels, it was dominated by the aged skeletal Maya god of death and putrefaction Ah Puch, meaning ‘flatulent one’ (fig. 4). Mesoamerican abundant funerary imaginary, recalled now on the Day of the Dead, was depicted in their artwork: skeletons, skulls, human carved bones, circular spots on the skin, closed dead eyes, open mouths, owls and bats, night and darkness, water and lilies. The skeletal remains, covered with cinnabar or red ochre, an iron or ferrum oxide like blood color, symbolized life and rebirth, and had the virtue to stop putrefaction. It was an expensive material like jade which was used to give vitality and associated with life because of its green color. A jade bead in the mouth of corpses, wrapped in cotton mantles and buried with maize gruel, signified the life spirit and served as money in the afterlife. In his Account of the things of Yucatan, Diego de Landa describes the ancient Mayan funerary practices.
Without fear of death, they reverenced their parents with wooden statues at home oratories. In the cult festivities, they offered them food and protection, being afraid of getting lost in the afterlife. Their souls, still alive, rested there, but this does not suggest any attempt to mummification.
Besides, the Inca Empire incorporated regional and ethnic diversity in a political achievement, including high degrees of technological, economic, socio-political and ideological development of previous Andean indigenous cultures. In Tawantisuyu, people believed in reincarnation and did not incinerate the corpses because their vital force would disappear, threatening their passage to the after world. Andean universe was divided in three different dimensions: Hanan pacha or ‘upper world, Kay pacha or surface world and Ujku pacha, the inner world, place of seeds and subterranean beings, where ancestors lived a new existence similar to the living, not being disturbed by calamities. Moche (500-700 AD) and Chimu (1000-1430 AD) funerary rituals introduced skeletons and fleshless creatures, who appeared in dances, parties and erotic poses without tragic sense, confirming that life after death was parallel to the living universe.
This resulted in the consequent transformation of the grave space. The last evolution structure in Peruvian tombs is shown in a complex of impressive burial towers built by the Kollas in the Inca period: the spectacular Chullpas of Sillustani on the shores of Lake Umayo near Puno. Popular beliefs considered tombs and rulers’ bodies as ‘huacas’, offering sacrifices and prayers to them. Based on a profound animism, sacred things had a spiritual power, including mountains, stones, rivers, caves and huacas.
The social prestige conferred by textiles made the fabrics grow in wealth, woven with fine cotton, gold and silver threads and vicuna wool.

Gods, myths, warriors, animals and plants were laid out in these coastal lords’ great coats and garments. All their palaces, wealth, land and possessions remained in their male descendants’ hands to support their cult for eternity. ‘Huacas’ were kept in ‘resting points’ or Zamana, a term meaning also mortuary caves. Funeral rituals, the most interesting Incan events, spanning from 1466 to 1634 AD, were restricted to kings, clan leaders and high nobles, the high social ranks (fig. 10). The Chinchorro mummies As the Inca Empire was expanding, it incorporated the beliefs and practices of conquered people.
Richard Latcham states in ‘Atacameño Archaeology’ : ‘old Beliefs die hard’. Chinchorro burial practices did not completely disappear with their culture. Soon after them, very similar practices were carried out by Atacameño people, inhabiting the northern part of Chile.
‘Their mummies, (in an extended position), were wrapped in skin of animals or sea birds’.
Provided the similarities between Chinchorro and Atacameño mummies, as well as the remarkable parallelism between these South American and Incan mortuary rituals, it is highly likely that the Andean royal practices were influenced, at least in part, by the Chinchorro, going from Atacameño culture directly to Incas, according to Latchman.
The name of this pre-ceramic and pre-metallurgical fishing society means ‘fishing boat’ (Chinchorro). They inhabited the arid coastal region of southern Peru and northern Chile, from Illo to Antofagasta, between 7020-1500 BC, including the Atacama Desert (fig. 11). Their oldest dissected corpses are dated around 7020 BC and the first treatments appeared in 5050 BC, reaching a peak about 3000 BC. In some cases, an embalmer would remove skin and flesh and replaced them with clay; in others, the internal organs were extracted and replaced with vegetable fibres or animal hairs. To him a Chinchorro mummy was either wrapped in a red mat or camelid skin shroud or covered with mud and buried naked or with a genital cover, laid on its back with legs extended or semiflexed.
